The region is especially famous for Malbec, the grape variety that has become a true symbol of Argentine winemaking. The combination of sunny days, cool nights, a dry climate and mountain water nourishing the vineyards creates ideal conditions for growing vines. Local wines are known for their depth of flavour, rich aromas and distinctive character, shaped by the land in which they are produced.

Exploring Luján de Cuyo would hardly be complete without travelling its wine routes. Visits to wineries offer a look behind the scenes of production, an introduction to centuries-old traditions and the finer points of winemaking, and an opportunity to enjoy regional cuisine. Many wineries welcome guests into inviting restaurants and onto open terraces overlooking vineyard-covered valleys and the Andean ranges.

Yet Luján de Cuyo has more to offer than food and wine. Nature lovers can explore mountain trails, the picturesque surroundings of Potrerillos and its expansive reservoir, and the thermal springs of Cacheuta, where relaxation comes with views of the mountains.

In Luján de Cuyo, wine culture becomes part of a wider journey through nature, tradition and gastronomy. Here you can enjoy the leisurely pace of life in the Argentine provinces, discover Mendoza's wealth of flavours and take home vivid memories of one of the country's most appealing regions.

Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel associated with the ruler Pachacuti. The complex is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

A visit focuses on stone houses, temples, plazas, walls, stairways and terraces. Notable landmarks include the Temple of the Sun, the Temple of the Three Windows, the Main Temple and the Intihuatana.

A journey to Machu Picchu is usually combined with Cusco and the Sacred Valley. The Inca Trail also leads to the citadel, crossing valleys and high mountain passes.

San Santiago Church stands in Machuca, a small high-altitude village in Chile's Atacama region. Dedicated to the village's patron saint, the church dates to the 19th century. Its adobe walls and thatched roof continue the building traditions of the surrounding houses, incorporating simple natural materials into the architecture.

According to the local cultural foundation Fundación Spa, the church is a centre for community celebrations featuring processions and traditional dances. A visit complements a walk through the village, where residents preserve crafts and pastoral traditions. On itineraries from San Pedro de Atacama, Machuca is a stop on the way back from the El Tatio geysers; nearby are high-altitude wetlands inhabited by birds.
